title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why does this module replace the task audit with a decision register?
options: Because tasks are harder to inventory accurately than decisions

Because the things carrying risk in a systems role are decisions that were made once, encoded, and abandoned while still executing — and a task audit cannot see them, since an encoded decision looks like a process step
Because 201's task audit was superseded by better practice
Because decisions are more frequent than tasks in People Operations work
questions.explanation: 201 M1's task audit is right for building a workflow you own. This is a different question, and the practical consequence is that you cannot enable AI on a decision nobody owns, because there is nobody to sign the enablement.

questions.prompt: What is the module's diagnostic question for identifying a deferred decision?
options: How often does this decision get made?
Is this decision documented anywhere?
Can you name the person — not the team — who would defend it if challenged?
Was this decision reviewed in the last twelve months?
questions.explanation: A team cannot sign anything, and Module 7 ends in a signature. "Nobody" is a valid and highly informative answer. D is a reasonable hygiene question and not the diagnostic.

questions.prompt: Where does HR technology management sit in AI adoption across HR practice areas? `[V]`
options: Roughly mid-pack, behind recruiting, L&D and employee experience
Second at around 21%, behind recruiting's 27% — inside a function where 54% of organizations have deployed no AI in HR at all and have no plans this year
Lowest, alongside compliance and board relations
Highest, ahead of recruiting
questions.explanation: From SHRM's 2026 mapping of 138 use cases across 16 practice areas, n=1,722. The pairing is the point: you are the front line of a function that mostly has not started, which makes "we haven't adopted AI yet" usually false in your stack specifically.

questions.prompt: Which of the three doors AI arrives through has no gate — and is the largest?
options: Employees using their own consumer tools
New product procurement
A feature arriving in a system you already own, via a release note
Pilot programs run by other functions
questions.explanation: Procurement is the only gated door and it receives essentially all governance attention. A is real and invisible but smaller. Nearly a third of organizations cannot say whether their current HR systems contain AI features, which is door one's signature.

questions.prompt: Why does the register require accountability by named person rather than by team?
options: Because individuals are more reliable than teams
Because a team cannot sign anything, and the track's final artifact is a decision-rights map with a signature line
Because regulators require named individuals for all HR decisions
Because team ownership is usually inaccurate in HR functions
questions.explanation: And resolving an honest blank by writing a plausible team name destroys the entry's value. C overstates the legal position; the reason is that a signature needs a signatory.

questions.prompt: What makes the wide-reach, long-latency quadrant the dangerous one?
options: Errors there are more frequent than in other quadrants

Nothing announces the failure, so the error runs across every transaction until an audit or a filing surfaces it — and this is precisely the quadrant AI is sold into, because the labour savings and the blast radius have the same cause
Those decisions are usually the highest-stakes ones
Regulators focus enforcement there
questions.explanation: Wide-reach short-latency failures are bad and they get fixed, because they announce themselves. C confuses stakes with the axes; the module's argument is that stakes are the wrong variable here.

questions.prompt: How does the module modify 201 M4's verification budget for systems work?
options: Verification should be doubled for any automated process
Size it to detection latency rather than only to stakes, because error cost compounds with every run before anyone notices
Verification should be sized to the number of people affected
Systems work needs no verification budget because logs provide an audit trail
questions.explanation: The same error rate costs wildly different amounts depending on when it surfaces — a nuisance if caught immediately, a year of transactions if caught at the annual audit. Same budget, different denominator.

questions.prompt: What does "AI can prepare and remind, but it cannot be the control" require in practice?
options: That a human performs every step of any process with a statutory deadline
That AI is never used for compliance-related work
That an automated control produce evidence it ran which somebody actually looked at — a reminder nobody acknowledged is a log entry, not a control
That controls be tested annually by internal audit
questions.explanation: Preparation is drafting, assembling, and flagging. The control is what guarantees the step happened, and guarantees need evidence. A prohibits far more than the rule requires.
